title: SlidesAI: Turning Notes Into Decks Where You Already Work
description: SlidesAI turns notes, PDFs and prompts into decks inside Google Slides, PowerPoint, ChatGPT or the web, with a brand kit that follows your deck.
content:
# SlidesAI: Turning Notes Into Decks Where You Already Work

The annoying part of AI presentation tools is rarely the generation. It is the round trip: paste text into a web app, wait, download a file, open it in PowerPoint, discover the theme is wrong, and restyle every slide by hand. SlidesAI's pitch is that the round trip should not exist, and the way it removes it is by living inside the four places people actually make decks.

## Four doors, one generator

[[link:/tools/1524|SlidesAI]] takes notes, documents, PDFs and plain prompts and returns a presentation. What distinguishes it is where that happens:

- **Google Slides** — build and edit slides inside Slides, no export step
- **PowerPoint** — create and refine without leaving the application
- **ChatGPT** — describe the deck in chat and have it saved to Google Slides
- **Web app** — paste content, get a deck, no install, works on mobile

The ChatGPT integration is the interesting one, because it changes the shape of the interaction. Instead of a form with fields, you have a conversation, and the output lands in Slides rather than in the chat window. For anyone already using ChatGPT for the thinking part, that is one fewer place to copy from.

The site claims 14M+ installs and 2,000+ reviews, and says it is used by companies and educational institutions. Those are vendor figures, not independently verified, but the install count is the kind of number that is hard to fake at this scale.

## The brand kit is the feature that matters

Anyone can generate a deck. The reason most generated decks get thrown away is that they look generated: default fonts, mismatched colours, layouts that do not match the company template.

SlidesAI's answer is a brand kit that reads your colours, fonts, logo and layouts from a PowerPoint file you upload, across 64 layouts. The site's own demonstration uses a consulting-style deck with a consistent serif heading font and a defined body font, and the claim is that every presentation comes out in those colours, fonts, logo and layouts with no restyling.

That is the right problem to solve. In an organisation where a deck has to match a house style, a generator that ignores the style is useless no matter how good the content is. The caveat is the obvious one: the kit is only as good as the file you feed it, and 64 layouts is a bounded vocabulary. Decks that depend on unusual compositions — dense charts, equations, annotated diagrams — will still need manual work, and the tool does not pretend otherwise.

The web app covers the case the plugins cannot: a phone. Building a deck from a document on mobile is otherwise a genuinely bad experience, and a browser route that needs no install is the difference between starting the deck on the train and starting it at the desk an hour later.

## What a generated deck is actually good for

The honest use case is the first draft, not the final one. If you have a document, a set of meeting notes or a research summary and you need something presentable in ten minutes, generation removes the blank-page tax. You then spend your time on the argument rather than on placing text boxes.

Where it helps least is the deck that carries the argument itself. A pitch whose structure is the persuasion, or a technical talk where the sequence of ideas is the point, will fight any template that decides structure for you. The generated version tends to produce the same shape every time: title, agenda, three points, summary. That shape is fine for a status update and wrong for a thesis.

For the writing half of the job, the choice is similar to other template-driven tools. [[link:/tools/1441|Nichesss]] handles copy formats with fixed structures, [[link:/tools/90|Grammarly]] cleans up prose you wrote, and SlidesAI handles the packaging step. They are not substitutes; they sit at different points in the same afternoon.

One practical detail the site does not address is what happens when the source document is badly structured. A PDF of scanned slides and a clean markdown outline produce very different decks from the same generator, and the difference is not the model's fault. Feeding it something with headings and short paragraphs is the cheapest quality improvement available.

## The trade, stated plainly

You get convenience and consistency, and you give up control over structure. You get four entry points and inherit four slightly different experiences, which is the usual cost of shipping everywhere. You get a brand kit and depend on having a well-built source deck to feed it.

For a team that produces a lot of routine decks — client updates, internal reviews, training material — that trade is easy to accept. For someone who makes four decks a year and cares about each one, a template and an afternoon may produce a better result than a generator that has to be corrected slide by slide.

Free to start, no card required, which is the correct way to find out which of those two people you are.
tldr: SlidesAI generates presentations from notes, documents, PDFs and prompts, and runs inside Google Slides, PowerPoint, ChatGPT and a web app rather than asking you to export and re-import. It claims 14M+ installs and 2,000+ reviews, and its brand kit reads colours, fonts, logos and layouts from a deck you upload, across 64 layouts. The constraint is that generated structure is still template structure.
